Volume 05 · Chapter 10

Externalities and public goods

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v05-c09

By the endCompare corrective instruments under informational and institutional constraints.

Price the missing effect, then check the institution

Capability: compare corrective instruments under informational and institutional constraints. Prerequisite: Contracts, incentives and organizations. We use competitive surplus accounting, the welfare qualifications in general equilibrium, and best responses from game theory. Every contribution and bargaining mechanism used below is specified locally.

A factory can pay for labor yet leave nearby residents to bear its smoke. A resident can enjoy a neighborhood warning system without paying for it. A driver pays for the time spent in a queue but can delay other drivers too. In each case, an individual choice leaves an effect outside that individual's decision account. Finding the omitted effect is the beginning: implementing a correction requires information, enforceable rules and a financing arrangement.

All numerical cases are original synthetic models, not observations or policy estimates. Unless an example states otherwise, quantities refer to one period; benefits, costs, transfers and surplus are dollars per period; marginal benefits and costs are dollars per unit of the corresponding activity. Coefficients carry the necessary units. Preferences are quasilinear in a common dollar numeraire, with sufficient wealth for the stated choices and transfers. Dollar benefits measure willingness to pay in that model. Unweighted total surplus is the stated efficiency criterion; it does not rank distributions ethically or imply that every person gains.

Private and social margins

An externality is a direct effect of one agent's activity on another agent's feasible production or well-being that the decision maker does not fully take into account through the relevant prices or agreement. A competitive price change redistributing purchasing power is not, by itself, an unpriced technological externality. Let Q be traded output, B(Q) buyers' gross benefit, C(Q) producers' real opportunity cost, and H(Q) damage borne by other people. Damage is a money equivalent of harm, not necessarily a cash payment. Define marginal benefit MB = B′, private marginal cost PMC = C′ and marginal damage MD = H′. The social marginal cost of output is SMC = PMC+MD.

Assume price-taking trade, no other distortions, efficient allocation among buyers and producers, and one measured unit of harmful emission per unit of output. An interior unregulated equilibrium satisfies MB(Q) = PMC(Q). Total surplus is W(Q) = B(Q)−C(Q)−H(Q), so a smooth interior efficient quantity satisfies MB(Q*) = PMC(Q*)+MD(Q*). This is a condition on the marginal unit, not on average damage H(Q)/Q. If W is concave on the feasible interval, the condition is sufficient; strict concavity gives uniqueness. At a zero-output optimum the right derivative must be nonpositive; at an upper capacity optimum the left derivative must be nonnegative. For nonconcave W, compare all candidates and boundaries.

A per-unit tax t creates a wedge between the buyer price pb and the seller's retained price ps: pb−ps = t. Interior competitive equilibrium then has MB(Q) = PMC(Q)+t. Thus t = MD(Q*) implements the efficient interior quantity under the stated assumptions. A constant corrective tax matches the missing margin at the target; it need not equal marginal damage at every possible output. The term Pigouvian tax denotes this correction. Revenue tQ transfers dollars to the recipient; collection expense and costly changes in behavior are separate real effects.

For an external benefit E(Q), with otherwise identical assumptions, surplus becomes B−C+E and the efficient condition is MB+E′ = PMC. A marginal subsidy E′(Q*) can align that margin if its funding and administration create no additional distortion. Existing monopoly power, distortionary finance, spillovers elsewhere or constrained instruments require a new joint problem. Adding a damage-based tax to an already distorted market does not automatically solve that problem.

The definitions and corrective-tax framework follow the method route in Emmanuel Saez's UC Berkeley externalities notes, particularly the private/social-margin and policy sections. The models and global arguments here supply their own assumptions and arithmetic.

Worked example 1 — A tax with a complete surplus account

A competitive product has MB = 84−2Q and PMC = 12+Q on 0 ≤ Q ≤ 42. Damage is H(Q) = Q²/2, so MD = Q. Integration with zero constants gives B = 84Q−Q² and C = 12Q+Q²/2. Without a correction, 84−2Q = 12+Q gives Q = 24 and price 36. The efficient objective is

W(Q) = 72Q−2Q² = 648−2(Q−18)².

Hence Q* = 18 is the unique global optimum. The tax is t = MD(18) = 18 dollars per unit. The new equilibrium has pb = 48, ps = 30, and revenue 18×18 = 324. Buyers' price rises by 12 and sellers' retained price falls by 6: the local linear-model incidence is two thirds on buyers and one third on sellers. Under the remittance-equivalence assumptions in Chapter 4, assigning the payment obligation to the other side does not change those prices.

Dollars per periodUnregulated Q = 24Taxed Q = 18
Consumer surplus B−pbQ576324
Producer surplus psQ−C288162
Public revenue0324
External damage288162
Total: CS+PS+revenue−damage576648

The gain is 72, not the revenue 324. CS falls by 252, PS falls by 126, the recipient obtains 324 and harm falls by 126; these changes sum to 72. The victims' gain is counted through reduced harm, even if they receive none of the revenue. An actual Pareto improvement additionally requires a feasible redistribution acceptable to the affected people.

Using MD at the old output would set t = 24, yielding Q = 16 and W = 640, eight below the maximum. Using total harm H(18) = 162 as the unit tax would confuse dollars per period with dollars per unit. Under a competitive market for permits, an enforceable cap of 18 units of emission instead induces a permit price of 18 and the same output. Auctioning permits produces revenue 324. Giving fixed, unconditional permits to existing owners transfers those scarcity rents to them; the permits still have an opportunity cost when used. The rent's recipient changes, while B−C−H at the same allocation does not.

A target, a cost allocation and an information problem

A quantity instrument limits aggregate activity or emissions. A tradable permit authorizes one measured unit; trade can equalize marginal control costs. A standard can instead specify each source's allowed emissions, required abatement or technology. A cap's efficiency target and its allocation across sources are separate questions. Competitive permit trade requires enforceable quantities, a functioning trading institution and no relevant market power or trading cost. Updating free allocations in response to current output can change incentives, unlike the fixed transfers in the worked example.

Heterogeneous abatement: why equal quantities need not minimize cost

Abatement aᵢ is the reduction from source i's specified baseline emission. Two sources each emit 12 units without control. They can choose 0 ≤ aᵢ ≤ 12, incur K₁(a₁) = a₁²/2 and K₂(a₂) = 3a₂²/2, and emit eᵢ = 12−aᵢ. Their marginal abatement costs are a₁ and 3a₂. Suppose a chosen total-emission limit of 12 requires a₁+a₂ = 12. Substituting a₂ = 12−a₁ gives

K₁+K₂ = 54+2(a₁−9)².

Thus a₁ = 9, a₂ = 3, emissions (3,9) and cost 54 are globally cost minimizing. Uniform abatement (6,6) costs 72, wasting 18 relative to this target. An emission charge τ = 9 makes each source minimize Kᵢ(aᵢ)+τ(12−aᵢ); each interior choice sets its marginal abatement cost equal to 9. A competitive cap-and-trade market with aggregate cap 12 has the same price and allocation. Tax receipts are 108, a transfer; the real abatement cost remains 54.

At a source's upper abatement bound, its marginal abatement cost can be below the common price: it would like to abate further but cannot. At a zero-abatement bound its marginal cost can be above that price. Equal marginal costs apply only to interior sources. The cost-saving argument assumes emissions have identical damage effects regardless of source; if location or timing changes harm, the socially relevant prices can differ. Nor does cost minimization prove that the selected aggregate cap of 12 is desirable: that requires benefits and damages as well.

Prices versus quantities when the state is unknown

Here is a fully specified uncertainty comparison. Let e be aggregate emissions, 0 ≤ e ≤ 20. Their private net benefit, before external damage, is V(e;A) = Ae−be²/2; damage is H(e) = de²/2, with b,d > 0. The regulator commits before learning A. A equals 10 or 14 with probability one half each; emitters learn A before choosing emissions. Slopes and probabilities are known, instruments are enforced without cost, and the regulator cannot revise them after the state is revealed. This is uncertainty about the private emissions-benefit schedule, equivalently the incentive to incur abatement cost.

In state A, W = Ae−(b+d)e²/2 and the unconstrained interior efficient emission is e*(A) = A/(b+d). Completing the square shows that the surplus loss at another emission e is exactly

L(e;A) = (b+d)[e−e*(A)]²/2.

With mean A₀ = 12 and b+d = 3, compare a fixed cap eC = 4 with the fixed nonnegative tax t = d×4. At these policies all state choices are interior. An emitter maximizes V−te; its bounded choice is eT(A) = min{20,max{0,(A−t)/b}}. The cap's expected-surplus objective is a concave quadratic on [0,20], maximized at 4. For each slope pair below and 0 ≤ t ≤ 10, no emission bound truncates (A−t)/b except possibly at the endpoint. Minimizing its expected squared error gives t = dA₀/(b+d); expected surplus is a concave quadratic on this tax interval. For t ≥ 10 the low state emits zero, and the high state emits at most 4/b, below its efficient 14/3 in both rows. Further tax increases reduce high-state surplus until emissions also reach zero at t = 14; surplus then remains zero. Thus no larger tax improves on t = 10, and the displayed interior choices are globally optimal among constant nonnegative taxes in this particular problem.

SlopesTaxTax emissions at A = 10,14Efficient emissionsExpected tax lossExpected cap loss
b = 2, d = 143, 510/3, 14/31/62/3
b = 1, d = 282, 610/3, 14/38/32/3

For example, the first tax misses each state optimum by 1/3, giving loss (3/2)(1/3)² = 1/6. The cap misses by 2/3. In the second row the tax misses by 4/3 and is worse than the cap. Steeper marginal damage makes fluctuations in emissions more costly in these cases. The reversal is established for the specified fixed instruments, information and linear margins; it is not a universal ranking. Damage uncertainty, threshold harms, correlated shocks, adaptive rules, evasion or different monitoring costs can change the comparison.

What must the instrument observe?

A tax on output is equivalent to an emission tax only when the output-emission mapping is fixed and known. If emissions are e = αQ and a producer can change intensity α, an output tax gives no direct reward for reducing α while holding Q fixed. An emission price does. A technology standard can sometimes be cheaper to verify but restrict the methods producers use; an emission price can allow more methods while requiring a credible emissions measure. Include the real costs of verification, administration and compliance in the comparison. Benefit and damage estimation also needs a causal model, a population, a time horizon and uncertainty analysis; a synthetically known MD curve is not evidence that a real authority knows it.

Hunt Allcott's MIT 14.42 Lecture 9 instructor notes, PDF pages 3–4, organize instrument comparisons around observability, control-cost heterogeneity, spatial effects and institutional constraints. The examples above and Exercise 8 make specific comparisons under explicitly supplied costs; they do not assert current regulatory practice.

A shared quantity requires vertical aggregation

A good is nonrival over a stated range if one person's use does not reduce the amount or quality available to another. It is nonexcludable under the available technology and institution if preventing nonpayers from benefiting is infeasible or prohibitively costly. A pure public good combines both properties. Government ownership is not its definition. An excludable but nonrival service is often called a club good; a difficult-to-exclude but rival resource is a common-pool resource. Congestion can make a facility rival at high use even if adding a user at low use causes little loss.

Let a common public-good quantity G benefit everyone. Person i has utility zᵢ+Bᵢ(G), where zᵢ is private numeraire, and provision costs CG(G) numeraire units. A feasible financing scheme collects payments Tᵢ satisfying ΣᵢTᵢ = CG(G). Total surplus is ΣᵢBᵢ(G)−CG(G). The derivative of this expression gives the interior Samuelson condition:

ΣᵢMBᵢ(G*) = CG′(G*).

The same increment dG is enjoyed by all, so its dollar marginal benefits add vertically at the same G. For a private good, consumers instead buy separate units: quantities add horizontally at a common price. If benefits are concave and cost convex, the public-good objective is concave; provision is zero when its right derivative at zero is nonpositive. A binding capacity may instead put the optimum at the upper boundary. Kinks require one-sided comparisons.

More generally, with smooth utility Uᵢ(zᵢ,G) and Uᵢ,z > 0, define MRSᵢ = Uᵢ,G/Uᵢ,z, the local numeraire compensation for one extra unit of G. A small increase dG can raise G while holding everyone locally indifferent by reducing each zᵢ by MRSᵢdG. The total available payment is ΣᵢMRSᵢdG. At a regular interior efficient allocation, with these numeraire reallocations feasible, it must equal the marginal resource requirement CG′dG; otherwise a small feasible change leaves resources for a gain. This establishes a local necessary condition ΣᵢMRSᵢ = CG′. Without quasilinearity the MRS values depend on the private allocation too; summing unweighted utility numbers is not a substitute.

Individual incentives need not satisfy that sum condition. In a voluntary-contribution game, each person chooses a nonnegative contribution gᵢ, pays for it, and obtains the total G = Σᵢgᵢ. A best response maximizes that person's payoff given the others' contributions. A Nash equilibrium is a profile where no individual can gain by changing only their own contribution. A nonpayer can enjoy the common benefit, creating a free-riding incentive. Equilibrium need not be zero provision; it also need not be efficient.

Saez's public-goods notes, PDF pages 2–8 and 11–15, provide the nonrival/nonexcludable distinction, vertical aggregation and voluntary-contribution framework. The financing comparisons below distinguish the efficient quantity from a mechanism that would deliver it.

Worked example 2 — Free riding, efficient provision and who finances it

Two residents have marginal benefits MB₁(G) = max{14−G,0} and MB₂(G) = max{10−G,0}. To define benefits at every possible G, set Bᵢ(G) = aᵢs−s²/2 with s = min{G,aᵢ}, a₁ = 14, a₂ = 10. Benefits therefore saturate rather than becoming negative at large G. One unit costs 6; each resident has initial numeraire 100. Voluntary contribution gᵢ costs 6gᵢ, and G = g₁+g₂. Feasible contributions are 0 ≤ gᵢ ≤ 100/6.

Person 1 maximizes B₁(g₁+g₂)−6g₁. Its derivative is MB₁(G)−6, decreasing until the benefit saturates and negative thereafter. The global best response is g₁ = max{0,8−g₂}; for person 2 it is g₂ = max{0,4−g₁}. These responses are below their wealth bounds. Both contributing positively would require G = 8 and G = 4 simultaneously. Only person 2 contributing would give (0,4), but person 1 would then add 4. Neither contributing is also unstable. Thus the unique equilibrium is (g₁,g₂) = (8,0).

At G = 8, gross benefits are (80,48), total cost is 48 and the residents' net benefits are (32,48), summing to 80. Person 2 benefits while paying nothing. For 0 ≤ G ≤ 10, efficient surplus is 18G−G² = 81−(G−9)², maximized at G = 9. For 10 ≤ G ≤ 14 its derivative is (14−G)−6 = 8−G < 0, and above 14 it is −6. The global optimum is therefore 9, where marginal benefits 5 and 1 sum to cost 6. Gross benefits are (85.5,49.5), cost is 54 and surplus is 81.

Equal fees of 27 deliver net benefits (58.5,22.5), making the earlier free rider worse off. To make both weakly better off than under voluntary contributions, require T₁+T₂ = 54, 85.5−T₁ ≥ 32 and 49.5−T₂ ≥ 48. These inequalities give 52.5 ≤ T₁ ≤ 53.5. Fees (53,1) yield net benefits (32.5,48.5), improving each by 0.5. Collection must be enforceable or otherwise agreed and implemented. Merely announcing these efficient fees does not make them a Nash outcome of the earlier voluntary game.

If the government first supplies G₀ using fixed lump-sum finance, preferences remain quasilinear and wealth stays sufficient, the remaining voluntary responses depend on G₀+g₁+g₂. For this example the equilibrium total is max{8,G₀}: additional public provision displaces person 1's contribution unit for unit until it reaches zero. Above that point total provision rises. This particular complete crowding-out result relies on the unchanged benefits, financing effects and contribution margins; it is not a general behavioral law.

The user pays an own cost and imposes an additional cost

Congestion concerns a rival use margin. Let n be trips per hour on a facility; ℓ(n) is each trip's generalized resource cost in dollars per trip, including travel time valued at the assumed common rate. Total hourly resource cost is nℓ(n). Differentiation gives marginal social cost ℓ(n)+nℓ′(n). An atomistic traveler takes the prevailing congestion as given and bears ℓ(n); the additional term nℓ′(n) is the delay cost an added trip imposes on existing travelers. Charging the entire social cost on top of the user's own cost would count that own cost twice.

Worked example 3 — A toll and its recipients

Trips have inverse marginal benefit P(n) = 30−n on 0 ≤ n ≤ 30. Own resource cost is ℓ(n) = 6+n/2. There are no other routes, network spillovers, administration expenses or heterogeneity in time valuation; trips are allocated to the highest-valued users. Untolled atomistic entry solves 30−n = 6+n/2, giving n = 16 trips per hour and own cost 14 dollars per trip.

Hourly benefit is B(n) = 30n−n²/2; resource cost is 6n+n²/2. Hence W(n) = 24n−n² = 144−(n−12)². Efficient flow is 12, own cost is 12, and the external marginal congestion cost is nℓ′ = 6. A toll of 6 gives generalized user price 18, exactly P(12). Toll receipts are 72 dollars per hour.

Without the toll, benefit is 352 and resource cost is 224, so surplus is 128. With it, benefit is 288 and resource cost is 144, so surplus is 144. User surplus after paying the toll is 288−12(12+6) = 72; adding receipts of 72 gives the same 144. Users collectively lose 56 before redistribution, while the recipient obtains 72 and total surplus rises by 16. Reduced congestion does not prove that every traveler is better off after paying the toll. The distributional conclusion depends on who travels and how receipts are used.

A congested road is not a pure nonrival public good on this use margin. Whether access is excludable depends on the available gate, charging technology and institution. Real networks, heterogeneous time values and uncertain travel times can require a richer model; these numbers establish no optimal toll for an actual facility.

Rights specify the disagreement point; bargaining needs a mechanism

The Coase bargaining benchmark asks whether affected parties can agree to internalize an external effect. A right specifies an enforceable entitlement and hence what happens without agreement. A transfer changes who receives dollars; a change in the harmful activity changes joint surplus. For bargaining to implement the largest available surplus, assume clear and enforceable rights, observable and contractible activity, complete information, negligible bargaining/enforcement cost, representation of all affected parties, feasible transfers and a bargaining process that actually reaches an efficient agreement. Quasilinear values keep marginal benefits and damages independent of the wealth redistribution. Rights alone do not supply that bargaining process.

The participation constraint for each party is that its agreed payoff be at least its disagreement payoff. A proposed activity with more joint surplus than disagreement permits a nonempty interval of individually acceptable transfers when unrestricted transfers are feasible. The interval's width equals the surplus gain. This is an existence statement about mutually acceptable agreements; strategic offers, private information, inability to commit or holdout can prevent the parties from selecting one.

Allcott's MIT 14.42 Lecture 6 instructor notes, PDF pages 2–3, discuss rights, bargaining costs, information and wealth effects; they also motivate comparing prices and quantities under uncertainty. Here transfer feasibility and agreement are checked explicitly rather than inferred from a rights assignment.

Worked example 4 — The same activity, different rights and payoffs

A producer chooses activity x ∈ [0,12]. Its net private benefit is V(x) = 24x−x². One neighbor suffers H(x) = x²/2. Payoffs below omit constant initial wealth. Activity is contractible, both parties know these functions, transfers are affordable and enforceable, and indifference is accepted. Joint surplus is

S(x) = 24x−3x²/2 = 96−(3/2)(x−8)².

The efficient activity is 8, with V(8) = 128 and H(8) = 32. First give the neighbor the right to zero activity. Disagreement is x = 0 and payoffs (0,0). If the producer pays the neighbor T for permission to choose x = 8, payoffs are (128−T,T−32). Both participate exactly when 32 ≤ T ≤ 128. The interval has width 96, the joint surplus gain. At T = 80 each receives 48.

Now give the producer the right to act without paying for damage. Its best disagreement choice maximizes V, so x = 12 and payoffs are (144,−72), with joint surplus 72. If the neighbor pays the producer R to reduce x to 8, payoffs are (128+R,−32−R). Participation requires 16 ≤ R ≤ 40. The interval has width 24, the surplus gain over this disagreement point. At R = 28 payoffs are (156,−60): each gains 12 relative to its own fallback.

Under both rights assignments an efficient agreement can implement x = 8. The payoff distributions differ radically. There is no claim that the harmed party prefers the second rights assignment, or that any split follows uniquely from efficiency. The neighbor's negative payoff records damage relative to its constant wealth, not a literal negative bank balance.

If negotiating and enforcing an agreement consumes a fixed real cost of 30, the second assignment offers at most 24 in gains and cannot finance that cost while preserving both disagreement payoffs. The first assignment offers 96 before that cost and can in principle finance it. Transaction costs can therefore break the invariance conclusion. A hard limit on the neighbor's payment can also prevent the unconstrained efficient bargain, as Exercise 7 demonstrates. Many affected parties, hidden valuations and noncontractible harm add further implementation constraints; they cannot be removed by assuming that the parties would benefit from agreement.

How to compare a proposed correction

Specify the activity, whose marginal effect is missing, the relevant population and the available alternatives. Derive the uncorrected behavior and an explicitly stated welfare target. Then solve behavior under each feasible instrument, including bounds, information, compliance, funding and administration. Reconcile benefits minus resource costs with the accounts of buyers, producers, victims and revenue recipients. Finally separate an efficiency comparison from incidence and from the evidence needed to estimate the primitives. This procedure may favor a tax, tradable cap, standard, negotiated contract or public financing in a particular case; a label alone cannot establish the result.

These models assume their benefit and damage schedules. Measuring a health effect, valuing an environmental change, predicting evasion, or identifying the effect of a public program requires the design and inference methods in Volume 4 and later field-specific evidence. Graduate public economics extends the analysis to heterogeneous preferences, distortionary taxation, incomplete information, dynamic pollution stocks and mechanism design. The present derivations establish the restricted models, not those general extensions.

Exercises

  1. A new corrective wedge. In a competitive market MB = 60−Q, PMC = 12+Q and MD = 2Q on 0 ≤ Q ≤ 60. Total benefit, private cost and damage have zero constants. Find the unregulated and efficient quantities, an implementing unit tax and both prices. Compute CS, PS, tax revenue and harm in each allocation. Prove the efficient choice is global and identify the net gain and incidence.
  2. A binding abatement limit. Use the two sources in the abatement section, but require total abatement 20. Find the global least-cost allocation, its cost and an implementing emission price. Compare uniform abatement of 10 each. Explain why equal marginal abatement costs would give an infeasible answer and what replaces that equality at the bound.
  3. Prove a bounded instrument ranking. In the uncertainty model let A have mean A₀, known b,d > 0, and assume every relevant choice is interior. Compare the fixed cap A₀/(b+d) and fixed tax dA₀/(b+d). Derive each state's surplus loss and their ratio when A ≠ A₀. Then take b = 3, d = 1 and equally likely A = 12,20, with 0 ≤ e ≤ 20. Find both policies, their emissions and expected losses. State two changes in assumptions for which your ratio does not establish a policy ranking.
  4. Public finance is part of the answer. Two people have MB₁ = max{10−G,0} and MB₂ = max{6−G,0}, unit provision cost 8 and sufficiently large numeraire wealth. Benefits have zero constants and saturate as in Worked example 2. Find the unique voluntary-contribution equilibrium and the efficient quantity, checking all benefit branches. Compute both people's equilibrium net benefits. Find a balanced fee pair for efficient provision that raises each net benefit by 2. Compare equal fees and explain why the balanced improving pair is not thereby implemented by voluntary contribution.
  5. Corners and crowding out. Return to Worked example 2. The government provides G₀ = 3 or G₀ = 10 before residents choose contributions. Its provision is financed by fixed lump-sum payments that leave wealth bounds slack. Solve each contribution equilibrium and total G. In a separate change with no government provision, raise unit resource cost to 25 and find efficient G. Explain why a subscription service that excludes nonpayers but serves an extra user at no resource or quality cost is not a pure public good under the definition used here.
  6. A different congestion schedule. Hourly inverse trip benefit is 42−n and own generalized resource cost is ℓ(n) = 6+n, with all other congestion assumptions unchanged. Find untolled flow, efficient flow, the corrective toll and receipts. Reconcile welfare directly with user surplus plus receipts in each case. Calculate the total gain and explain why setting the toll equal to the full marginal social cost would double-count an existing cost.
  7. A constrained bargain. Use the producer-rights case in Worked example 4, but impose a hard upper bound R ≤ 9 on the neighbor's payment. Only reductions x ∈ [0,12] with nonnegative R are contractible; the producer retains its disagreement payoff 144 and accepts indifference. There are no bargaining costs. Find the greatest joint surplus feasible under both participation constraints and the payment bound. Give x, R, both payoffs and the efficiency loss relative to unrestricted bargaining. Separately restore unrestricted transfers and impose a fixed real agreement cost 30. Can an individually acceptable agreement improve on disagreement?
  8. Measurement can reverse an instrument choice. A plant must supply a fixed contractual output of 10 units. Its only choices are a dirty technology with emission intensity 0.8 and zero extra resource cost, or a clean technology with intensity 0.2 and extra resource cost 50. Harm is 15 dollars per emission unit. All common production costs and benefits cancel; behavior and enforcement are certain. Compare no policy, an output tax of 3 dollars per output unit, and an emission tax of 15 dollars per emission unit. Which technology is privately chosen, and what is the real surplus gain before policy administration? Now suppose implementing the emission tax costs 60 per period in real monitoring resources, while a verified clean-technology standard costs 5 and induces compliance. Compare these policies with no policy, count revenue correctly, and identify one missing fact needed before transferring the recommendation to an actual plant.
Complete solutions

  1. Unregulated trade solves 60−Q = 12+Q, so Q = 24 and p = 36. Here B = 60Q−Q²/2, C = 12Q+Q²/2 and H = Q². Thus W = 48Q−2Q² = 288−2(Q−12)², globally maximized at Q* = 12. Set t = MD(12) = 24, giving pb = 48 and ps = 24. The buyer price rises by 12 and seller price falls by 12, so each side bears half of the wedge in this model.

    Without tax, CS = 24²/2 = 288, PS = 24²/2 = 288, revenue = 0 and harm = 24² = 576; total surplus is zero. With tax, CS = 72, PS = 72, revenue = 24×12 = 288 and harm = 144; total is 288. The changes −216−216+288+432 sum to the gain 288. Positive private gains at the unregulated allocation were exactly offset by the specified external damage; zero total surplus there does not mean no one benefited.

  2. With a₂ = 20−a₁, feasibility requires 8 ≤ a₁ ≤ 12. Total cost is a₁²/2+3(20−a₁)²/2 = 150+2(a₁−15)². The unconstrained minimizer 15 is outside this interval; the nearest feasible value is a₁ = 12, giving a₂ = 8 and cost 72+96 = 168. Emissions are (0,4). Uniform (10,10) costs 50+150 = 200, 32 more.

    At an emission price τ = 24, source 2 chooses a₂ = 24/3 = 8; source 1 would like a₁ = 24 but is limited to 12. Its marginal cost 12 is below 24 at the bound. It cannot shift one further unit of abatement from the costly second source to itself. A common-price allocation therefore has equality for source 2 and the appropriate inequality for source 1. Receipts would be 24×4 = 96, separate from the control cost.

  3. Write Δ = A−A₀. The efficient choice is A/(b+d). The cap error is −Δ/(b+d). Since eT = [A−dA₀/(b+d)]/b, its error is dΔ/[b(b+d)]. Inserting these into L = (b+d)(e−e*)²/2 gives LC = Δ²/[2(b+d)] and LT = d²Δ²/[2b²(b+d)]. For Δ ≠ 0 their ratio is (d/b)²; at Δ = 0 both losses are zero and the ratio 0/0 is undefined. With nonzero finite variance and all choices interior, the same ratio holds for expected losses.

    For the supplied values A₀ = 16, cap = 4 and tax = 4. Efficient emissions are 3 and 5. Tax emissions are 8/3 and 16/3. The cap errors are +1 and −1, giving expected loss 2. Tax errors are −1/3 and +1/3, giving expected loss 2/9. The tax has lower expected loss in this model. Binding emission bounds, random damage slopes correlated with A, nonlinear threshold harm, instrument-specific monitoring costs or policies revised after A is observed can invalidate this calculation; any two with an explanation of the changed choice or loss formula suffice.

  4. The best responses are g₁ = max{0,2−g₂} and g₂ = max{0,−2−g₁} = 0. Thus the unique equilibrium is (2,0), with G = 2, benefits (18,10), payment (16,0) and net benefits (2,10). Efficient surplus on 0 ≤ G ≤ 6 is (16−8)G−G² = 16−(G−4)², maximized at 4. On 6 ≤ G ≤ 10 its derivative is 10−G−8 = 2−G < 0; above 10 it is −8. So 4 is the global optimum.

    At G = 4, benefits are (32,16), total cost is 32 and total surplus 16, four above the equilibrium value 12. Fees (28,4) give net benefits (4,12), each two above its equilibrium net benefit. Equal fees (16,16) give (16,0), reducing person 2's net benefit by 10. The improving fees balance the resource budget and satisfy participation relative to equilibrium, but person 2's unilateral best response in the original game remains zero. An enforceable or successfully agreed financing mechanism is additional structure.

  5. With G₀ = 3 the responses are g₁ = max{0,5−g₂} and g₂ = max{0,1−g₁}. Both positive would require two different total targets, so the unique equilibrium is (5,0), giving total G = 8. With G₀ = 10 both responses are zero; total G = 10. Crowding out is complete in the first comparison with no government provision, but the nonnegativity bound stops further displacement once private provision is exhausted. Fixed financing and slack wealth are essential to using the same response targets.

    With unit cost 25, the sum of marginal benefits at zero is 14+10 = 24 < 25, and it only decreases as G rises. Efficient G is zero. For the subscription service, use is nonrival over the specified range but access is excludable: it is a club-good case, not a pure public good. Neither public ownership nor private ownership by itself determines these properties.

  6. Untolled flow solves 42−n = 6+n, giving n = 18, own cost 24 and total benefit 42×18−18²/2 = 594. Resource cost is 18×24 = 432, so welfare and user surplus are 162. Marginal social cost is ℓ+nℓ′ = 6+2n. Efficient flow solves 42−n = 6+2n, giving n = 12. Equivalently W = 36n−3n²/2 = 216−(3/2)(n−12)² proves global efficiency.

    At 12, own cost is 18, the external marginal cost and toll are 12, and user price is 30. Benefit is 432, resource cost 216, toll receipts 144 and user surplus 432−12×30 = 72. Thus 72+144 = 216 equals benefit minus resource cost; the gain is 54. The full marginal social cost is 30, of which the user already bears 18. Charging 30 in addition to that own cost would produce a generalized price of 48 at this proposed flow and would not support it.

  7. To preserve the producer's payoff, R ≥ 144−V(x) = (12−x)². Together with R ≤ 9 and 0 ≤ x ≤ 12 this requires x ≥ 9. Joint surplus S = 96−(3/2)(x−8)² decreases as x moves above 8, so among these feasible activities it is maximized at x = 9. At that point R must be 9. The producer receives V(9)+9 = 135+9 = 144. The neighbor receives −81/2−9 = −99/2 = −49.5, above its fallback −72, so its participation is satisfied. Total surplus is 189/2 = 94.5, below 96 by 3/2. This constructs a feasible constrained optimum; relaxing the neighbor's participation in the initial bound did not produce an infeasible final candidate.

    With unrestricted transfers but real agreement cost 30, the largest surplus after paying that cost is 96−30 = 66, below disagreement surplus 144−72 = 72. Both participation constraints cannot hold simultaneously. No transfer changes that sum, so there is no individually acceptable costly agreement improving on disagreement. This conclusion concerns the given producer-rights fallback.

  8. Dirty emissions are 8 and clean emissions are 2. Without policy the plant chooses dirty because clean adds cost 50. An output tax charges 30 under either technology, leaving dirty privately preferred. It changes the payment recipient but creates no real surplus gain here because the output is fixed and the technology does not change.

    An emission tax costs the plant 120 with dirty technology and 50+30 = 80 with clean technology, so it chooses clean. The damage falls from 120 to 30 while resource production cost rises by 50: the gain is 120−30−50 = 40 before administration. The clean outcome's tax receipt of 30 is a transfer; adding it as an extra benefit to 40 would double-count. Private compliance costs already include the payment, while social resource costs do not.

    With monitoring cost 60, the emission-tax gain relative to no policy is 40−60 = −20. The verified clean standard achieves the same physical change at cost 5, giving gain 35. Among the specified alternatives, the standard has the highest surplus, the output tax has zero physical gain before any unprovided administration expense, and the emission tax reduces surplus once its supplied monitoring cost is included. This ranking presumes certain compliance and the stated feasible technologies. Actual harm per unit, verification cost, unobserved compliance, technology availability or responses of output would require evidence before applying the conclusion; identify at least one and explain which term or behavior it would change.

Teach-back

Explain to a colleague why a tax equal to marginal damage can improve total surplus even when both buyers and sellers lose, and why an efficient public-good quantity does not determine who should pay. Then distinguish a pure public good from congestion, and explain the role of the disagreement point in a bargain.

Teach-back evaluation and illustrative answer

A complete explanation identifies the previously omitted effect, states the competitive and quasilinear assumptions, balances the recipient's revenue against private payments, and measures the gain as benefits minus all real costs and harm. Public-good efficiency sums marginal benefits at the same quantity; financing must separately satisfy budget balance and any participation or distributional requirements. Congestion makes additional use costly to others, so the toll targets the external part beyond the user's own cost. Rights determine fallback payoffs and acceptable transfer intervals. Clear rights permit the benchmark only with feasible transfers, contracting and successful bargaining; efficiency does not erase distribution.

Delayed check

After several days, without rereading, take MB = 40−Q, PMC = 4+Q and MD = Q on 0 ≤ Q ≤ 40, with zero constants in the integrated functions. Find the unregulated quantity, efficient quantity, tax, buyer and seller prices, revenue and total-surplus gain. Explain why substituting total damage for the tax has the wrong units. Name one reason a mathematically correct tax target may fail to be the preferred implementable instrument.

Delayed-check answer

Unregulated Q = 18 and p = 22. Social surplus is 36Q−3Q²/2 = 216−(3/2)(Q−12)², so Q* = 12 and t = 12. Buyer price is 28, seller price 16 and revenue 144. Unregulated surplus is 162 and corrected surplus 216, a gain of 54. At the optimum total damage is 72 dollars per period, whereas marginal damage and the unit tax are 12 dollars per unit; they measure different objects. Expensive measurement, unenforceable emissions, other distortions, uncertain damage or instrument-specific administration can require a different implementable comparison.

Sources and further study

  • Emmanuel Saez, UC Berkeley Economics 131 — Externalities — Primary instructor method route for direct external effects, private/social marginal costs and benefits, Pigouvian correction at the efficient quantity, permit rents and heterogeneous control costs. Original chapter examples independently derive their objectives, global optima and transfer/resource accounts.
  • Emmanuel Saez, UC Berkeley Economics 131 — Public Goods — Primary instructor route for nonrivalry/nonexcludability, vertical marginal-benefit aggregation, the Samuelson condition, voluntary-contribution best responses and bounded crowding out. The chapter supplies original saturating benefits, active-set equilibrium proof and explicit efficient financing/participation calculations.
  • Hunt Allcott, MIT 14.42 — Lecture 6 Instructor Notes, Coase and Cap-and-Trade — Primary course route for enforceable rights, alternative payment directions, transaction costs, information and wealth effects in Coase bargaining; also the scoped price/quantity comparison when private control incentives are uncertain. Chapter bargaining intervals and quadratic state-loss identities are independently constructed.
  • Hunt Allcott, MIT 14.42 — Lecture 9 Instructor Notes, Risk, Uncertainty and Liability — Primary instructor checklist for instrument comparisons involving observable emissions versus inputs, heterogeneous abatement costs, spatial damages, market power, enforcement and uncertainty. Supports the need to specify instrument information and administration, not the numerical ranking of any actual policy.
